Issued at 340 PM EST Wed Nov 25 2026

===== Soaking Rain Expected for Thanksgiving =====

For this afternoon, some breaks in the cloud deck are noted on GOES 
imagery as a semi-dry slot works into central KY. This has led to a 
wide temperature range across the area, with near 60F around Lake 
Cumberland, but only low 40s in our north. Drier weather will 
persist for a few more hours, but we'll see an influx of moisture 
by tonight, with PWATs rising over 1 inch from south to north by 
tomorrow morning. 

On a synoptic scope, a longwave trough has been analyzed through 
upper air data, with an upper low embedded within that is over 
northwestern MO/southeastern NE. Two vorticity maxima are noted on 
mesoanalysis, one being tied to the upper low over the Midwest, and 
the second near the base of the longwave trough across the Gulf 
Coast. Through tonight, the upper trough will deepen into a 
secondary upper low across the South, and eventually leading to 
these two upper lows and associated vort maxes to merge into one 
over the Ohio Valley by Thursday night. Lower in the column, an 
easterly 35-45kt LLJ is pulling moisture inland from the mid-
Atlantic, which will aid in our PWAT surge overnight. At the sfc, an 
inverted sfc trough is stretching across the TN/OH Valleys, with a 
700mb frontogenesis band beginning to set up over southwestern IL 
and southeastern MO. This FGEN band will be the primary driver for 
snow bands to dump heavy wet snow across the St. Louis area.

For our area, widespread soaking rain, and perhaps some snowflakes 
mixing in, will be on the menu for Thanksgiving and into Friday 
morning. Beginning later tonight, we'll see rainfall spread 
northward through our area as a coastal sfc low moves into the mid-
Atlantic region, amplifying our moisture advection as the inverted 
trough provides a localized focus for lift. Expect precip to remain 
as all rain tonight as WAA keeps our temps in the 40s.  

Widespread rain and breezy winds are expected all day on 
Thanksgiving, with highs only in the upper 40s. This combination 
will make for quite a soggy and brooding day. The trend with the 
forecast has been to delay and decrease any rain-snow mix chances, 
mainly due to the southwestern shift in the FGEN band pivot near St. 
Louis and the cold air wrap around. Confidence has been increasing 
on seeing this colder air filter into the TN Valley, resulting in 
better chance for snowflakes to our south. However, this does not 
clear our area from any light snow mixing in with rain, but does 
better confine those chances to mainly being along and south of the 
WKY/BG Parkways. Also, given the temperature profiles, do not expect 
to see any snow mixing in until late Thursday night or into early 
Friday morning when our temps cool. One caveat to this would be if 
we see any heavier precip rates Thursday afternoon or evening, which 
would support some snow making it to the sfc, but REFS 1-hr precip 
rates do not hint at any high rates through the daytime. 

By Friday morning, the backside of the system will be spinning 
through, and with the timing of our diurnal min temps, could see 
some light rain-snow mix or a switch over to light snow. However, 
due to the warm soil temps and sfc temps remaining above freezing, 
no impacts or accumulations are expected. 

This system will bring a healthy amount of rain to the area though, 
which will be beneficial to our drought conditions. The widespread 
rain will bring 1-2 inches of rain steadily over the course of 24-36 
hours, which will be great for soaking into the ground and hopefully 
alleviate some of the drought. Given the steadiness of light to 
brief moderate rain, with no isolated downpours expected, there is 
no concern for flash flooding tonight or tomorrow in the area. The 
probability for over 1 inch of rain across the entire area is over 
90%, and over 2 inches being a 50-60% chance west of I-65. 


===== More Rain on Sunday =====

Expect the upper level regime to take on a more zonal approach by 
the weekend, with dry weather set to return and temps in the 50s. 
However, another shortwave trough will pivot across the central US, 
leading to another frontal boundary raising precip chances in our 
area by Sunday. Model soundings do not show much of any instability, 
but could see some higher shear if a sfc low passes nearby. Still a 
bit too early to get into amounts, but this system will not be as 
strong as our Thanksgiving forecast. The rest of the forecast looks 
to remain mainly dry and seasonable for late November as sfc high 
pressure builds in over the region for the start of the week.
